h: רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר, מַאֲמָר ח׳ Rosh Chodesh Adar — Maamar Ches

p: And according to the version of the Geonim,
in the count of the twelve powers
the power of sleep is the twelfth,
and the reading is: "He made Kuf king over sleep,
and these and these are the words of the living G-d.
For the work of this month is
that even in sleep Yisrael are Kuf, holy,
since they are bound at the root
And this is according to what they said
"I am asleep from the mitzvos, etc.,
but my heart is awake to do them, etc.
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
that HaKadosh Baruch Hu is the heart of Yisrael?
and my portion is Elokim forever.'"
That is, from the side of Hashem Yisbarach:
"There is none who knows how to slander
and we said this means that he knew
and he said, "They are asleep from the mitzvos;
and he said, "And the laws of the King
it serves for both the holy and the mundane
that they do not perform the commandment
And "they are asleep from the mitzvos" —
since it was written in a verse,
presumably there was some basis for his accusation,
for Scripture does not record words of falsehood
even though it is true that he said them,
as we demonstrated from the Midrash
And so we have seen that his accusation was effective,
only it was a seal of clay
He made Kuf king over sleep,
who is the heart of Yisrael —
since they are bound at the root;
and therefore it is the time
for eradicating the "first" of the kelipah,
And it is written (Shir HaShirim, ibid.),
for My head is filled with dew" —
this refers to Torah she'b'al peh,
which is the dew of Atika,
the dew with which HaKadosh Baruch Hu is destined
And this is "and my heart is awake":
Hashem Yisbarach rouses Yisrael from sleep
And the Ra'avad, of blessed memory,
when he matched the twelve powers
(וְנִתְבָּאֵר רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ כִּסְלֵו מַאֲמָר ד עַיֵּין שָׁם)
(as explained for Rosh Chodesh Kislev, maamar 4, see there);
and likewise Shlomo, peace be upon him,
that King Shlomo, peace be upon him,
and this is Kuf, the lower holiness,
the wisdom of Shlomo, in sleep.
And this comes from the side of Hashem Yisbarach,
in the manner that it says,
"The voice of my Beloved knocks: open for Me" —
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה שָׁם, ג).
(as stated in Shir HaShirim Rabbah, ibid. 3);
[פְּרִי צַדִּיק לְרֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ שְׁבָט מַאֲמָר ד]
that at first there is needed
an arousal from below, at least,
to do teshuvah out of fear,
willful sins become for him like unintentional ones;
and then Hashem Yisbarach, on His part,
which indicates, "From the outset you were merely wayward"
That is, Hashem Yisbarach rouses us
to do teshuvah out of love,
whereby the sin is uprooted at its root,
for "from the outset you were merely wayward";
and on the contrary, they even become for him like merits,
from the verse "because of them he shall live"
is called "those who fear My Name"
(יְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּמַאי פֶּרֶק ד הֲלָכָה א טז, ב):
"The awe of Shabbos is upon the am ha'aretz" —
Shabbos is a time of teshuvah,
"It is good to give thanks, etc.,"
"but he who confesses and forsakes them will be shown mercy."
And then is the time to merit,
from the side of Hashem Yisbarach,

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Resisei Layla 29:1 — “Although a person is drowsy, and in drowsiness has no heart, for a person cannot remain firmly at his station and the heart’s first powerful awakening weakens with time, the counsel is: ‘Commit your works to the Lord, and your thoughts will be established.’ For the blessed God does not become drowsy. This is the meaning of ‘I sleep, but my heart is awake,’ which our Sages explained: the Holy One, blessed be He, is called Israel’s heart.... He is awake to give life to the deeds a person performs as though drowsy.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: This identifies the “awake heart” with God’s continuing support when human spiritual attention weakens. It clarifies why the maamar treats sleep as concealment of an enduring bond rather than the disappearance of that bond.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2 — “The congregation of Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: ‘Master of the world, I sleep from the commandments, but my heart is awake to acts of kindness. I sleep from acts of charity, but my heart is awake to perform them. I sleep from the sacrifices, but my heart is awake to the recitation of Shema and prayer. I sleep from the Temple, but my heart is awake to synagogues and houses of study. I sleep from the end, but my heart is awake to redemption. I sleep from redemption, but the heart of the Holy One, blessed be He, is awake to redeem me.’ Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said: ‘Where do we find that the Holy One, blessed be He, is called the heart of Israel? From the verse, ‘God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever.’’”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados, Megillah 13b — “It should have written only ‘yesh’; therefore they expounded ‘yeshno’ — either they change their mitzvos … ‘one people’: just as the rest are not in mitzvos, so the Rabbanan.” Maharsha shows the textual basis for the accusation Rav Tzadok builds on. The extra letters of the verse itself carry Haman's charge of sleep and his denial that the Sages' merit protects the people.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Va'eira 14 — “Amalek is the kelipah of the dog, as the holy Zohar says … all the accusations Haman spoke, he meant as accusations against them above: ‘they are asleep from the mitzvos.’” Rav Tzadok shows that Haman's slander is Amalek's essential kelipah, the accuser on high. He adds that at the third Shabbos meal, as on Yom Kippur, it has no permission to accuse.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Tzav 2 — “Korach claimed, ‘All the congregation are holy, and Hashem is in their midst.’ And this is true, for otherwise the Torah would not write the false words that Korach said.” Rav Tzadok applies the same rule to Korach: words of the wicked recorded in Scripture still contain truth. Haman's charge that Yisrael “sleep from the mitzvos” therefore had real grounds, and the remedy is found in the hidden holiness of the heart, not in denying the charge.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Toldot 1 — “Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai said: Great is peace, for the Torah spoke untrue words for the sake of peace. Which words? ‘Thus shall you say to Joseph: Please forgive your brothers’ transgression and sin.’ We do not find that Jacob commanded any of these things; rather, he knew Joseph’s piety and would not suspect him or regard him as a shedder of blood.” Rav Tzadok refers to an inference developed elsewhere from this exceptional treatment of an untrue report for the sake of peace. The Midrash does not state his general principle in those exact words.

paragraphs.text: Esther Rabbah 7:13 — “Moses said: ‘Is there a worthy man in that generation?’ Elijah answered, ‘There is, and his name is Mordechai.’ Moses said: ‘Go and inform him, so that he will stand in prayer there and I here, and we will seek mercy for them before the Holy One, blessed be He.’ Elijah said: ‘Faithful shepherd, a decree of destruction has already been written against Israel.’ Moses said: ‘If it is sealed with clay, our prayer is heard; if it is sealed with blood, what has happened has happened.’ He answered: ‘It is sealed with clay.’ Moses our teacher said: ‘Go and inform Mordechai.’”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 19:10–12 — “This exile of the soul's wisdom affects only the influence extending from it throughout the soul to give it life. The root and essence of this wisdom in the divine soul, however, is in the mind. It is not actually clothed in exile within the sackcloth of the kelippah in the heart's left chamber; rather, in the wicked it is asleep and does not act upon them while their thought and understanding are occupied with worldly desires. But when they face a trial in faith, which is above knowledge, and it touches the soul's wisdom, this wisdom awakens from sleep and acts through God's power clothed within it, as it says, 'Hashem awoke as one asleep.' They then withstand the test without any reason, knowledge or intellectual explanation they can grasp. … Although the kelippos have overpowered them throughout their lives, when the test concerns faith in the one God, all the kelippos are nullified before the divine light clothed in the soul's wisdom.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Tanya distinguishes the soul's outward influence, which can be captive to wrongdoing, from its essential wisdom, which remains only dormant. This supplies a precise model for Rav Tzadok's conjunction of a valid charge against Israel's conduct and an untouched holy root. Tanya also identifies a test that reaches faith beyond reason as the trigger for sudden awakening even after lifelong failure—a further dimension of the existential decree described here. The two authors locate the recovery in a root deeper than the conduct exposed to accusation, without denying the reality of that conduct.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, 149b–150a (Vayetzei) — “It is written, ‘The Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream of the night, and God said: Ask what I should give you.’... Here one level was included within another, a higher level within a lower level, because Solomon had not yet attained completeness. Once he attained completeness, it is written, ‘The Lord gave wisdom to Solomon,’ and, ‘Solomon’s wisdom increased.’ The moon stood in its fullness and the Temple was built. Then Solomon saw wisdom eye to eye and did not need a dream.”

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 4:1 — “The verse alludes: ‘Return, wayward children,’ which they explained: ‘You were wayward from the outset.’ Repentance is a cure retroactively, unlike a person whose blemish has merely healed. After deliberate sins have become like inadvertent sins through repentance from fear, arising from the person below, the blessed God arouses from above: ‘Return, wayward children—you were wayward from the outset,’ to bring about repentance from love.... He becomes repaired from his very beginning.”

paragraphs.text: Taanit 8b — “Rabbi Yitzchak said: Sunshine on the Sabbath is charity for the poor, as it is said, ‘For you who fear My name, a sun of charity shall rise, with healing.’” The Gemara applies Malachi’s words “you who fear My name” to those who benefit from Sabbath sunshine. Rav Tzadok draws out the Sabbath’s awakening of reverence within every Jew.

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem Talmud Demai 4:1 — “The colleagues said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: They permitted it out of honor for the Sabbath.... Rabbi Bibi said in Rabbi Chanina’s name: The awe of the Sabbath rests upon him, and he speaks the truth. If the awe of the Sabbath rests upon him, why does the Mishnah teach that after nightfall at the Sabbath’s conclusion one may not eat until tithing? Because of the person upon whom the awe of the Sabbath does not rest.” The legal case concerns produce purchased from a person who is not generally trusted about tithing. His Sabbath answer is trusted in the circumstances specified by the Mishnah; the passage also records a qualification to the Sabbath-awe explanation.
